newsitem.title: USA: QVC TV leads U.S. gold jewelry sales rise in 1996.
newsitem.headline: QVC TV leads U.S. gold jewelry sales rise in 1996.

text.p: U.S. television shopping channel QVC Inc led the rise in gold jewelry sales among non-store retail distribution channels in 1996 with a 14 percent jump to more than $450 million, QVC vice president for jewelry merchandising John Calnon said Monday.

"QVC is now the world's largest retailer of 14-karat gold jewelry, with jewelry accounting for 30 percent of the electronic retailers 24 hour-a-day, 364 day-a-year, live television programming," Calnon told journalists at a briefing ahead of QVC's launch of its "Arte D'Oro" collection Monday evening.

In some recent television programs, QVC sold more than $1 million of gold jewelry an hour over a 24-hour period, more than some traditional jewelry stores sell in a year, World Gold Council chief executive for the America's Michael Barlerin said.
QVC is probably the largest retailer of 18-karat gold jewelry in the U.S., he said.
QVC is the largest electronic retailer in the U.S. and total sales last year reached $1.8 billion after receiving 80 million phone calls at an average of 192,000 a day.
Last year saw the fifth consecutive year of increases in gold jewelry sales in the U.S., with total sales reaching $12.3 billion, up five percent from 1995, Barlerin said.
This performance kept pace with non-auto U.S. retail sales as a whole which were also up five percent last year.

Though dollar and unit sales were up in virtually every distribution channel, the U.S. gold jewelry market mirrored overall retail trends and displayed a share shift from small traditional jewelry retail outlets to mass retailers.
Gold sales among non-traditional retail channels (discount stores, department stores and non-store retailers such as QVC) now account for 53 percent of total gold jewelry sales, Barlerin said.

Discount stores led the sales rise among categories of distribution channels in 1996 with a gain of 10 percent, while department store dollar sales were up eight percent and non-store retailers, such as catalogue and electronic retailers, increased five percent to $1.1 billion.
Total gold jewelry sales in the U.S. have risen to $12.3 billion in 1996 from $9.9 billion in 1992.

The average price of $86 paid for a piece of gold jewelry in retail stores has remained virtually constant over the past five years, while about 70 percent of gold jewelry was purchased by women for themselves or as gifts for others.
Gold jewelry accounts for the majority of gold demand in the U.S. while internationally gold jewelry demand has been outstripping world gold mine production in the 1990s, Barlerin said.
